response:
The model lmer(rt ~ condition + (1 | subject)) includes only a random intercept for subjects, but condition is manipulated within subjects. This means each subject sees multiple levels of condition, so subjects can — and typically do — vary not just in their overall mean RT but in how strongly they respond to the condition manipulation. Omitting the by-subject random slope for condition ((1 + condition | subject)) is a meaningful modeling error.

The specific problem is that when a within-subjects predictor varies within the random-effect grouping factor, a random-intercepts-only model treats the residual variance incorrectly. The effect of condition is estimated using within-subject variability, but without a random slope, the model does not account for the fact that subjects differ in their condition effect. This deflates the standard error of the condition fixed effect, inflating the t-statistic and producing anti-conservative (inflated) Type I error rates for that within-subjects effect.

This issue is well-documented. Barr, Levy, Scheepers, & Tily (2013, 'Keep It Maximal,' Journal of Memory and Language) showed that random-intercepts-only models for within-unit predictors substantially inflate Type I error — in some simulations well above the nominal 5% level — and recommended fitting the maximal random-effects structure justified by the design. Schielzeth & Forstmeier (2009, Behavioral Ecology) made a similar point. The practical upshot: a p-value of 0.02 from this model is not trustworthy because the model is anti-conservative for the very effect being tested.

The analysis as fit is not defensible as the primary inferential model. The correct approach is to refit with lmer(rt ~ condition + (1 + condition | subject)). If that model fails to converge or produces singular fits (common with limited data), options include simplifying the correlation structure ((1 + condition || subject)), using a Bayesian mixed model with weakly informative priors, or at minimum reporting the limitation prominently and treating the result as preliminary. Simply noting p = 0.02 without addressing the random-slope omission would be a reviewable flaw.
